1a:
**Sub-item 1a (2 points) — was the meaning of a cumulative KPISet discussed?**

Apply this item as a pure presence check, not a correctness check and not a depth check. Do not deduct as long as the answer conveys, in any defensible way, what a cumulative KPISet is or what role it plays — whether by describing it as the result of merging two or more KPISets, or by any other coherent account such as its holding aggregate statistics covering the whole test run rather than a single interval. The merging mechanism specifically is not required. A passing mention is enough: a single clause while explaining other code, e.g. "self.cumulative, which merges all KPISets," identifies it as the merged/overall set and earns no deduction; no elaboration is required.

Likewise, do not deduct when the answer does explain the cumulative KPISet but explains it wrongly — e.g. calling it deduplication, or describing it as aggregation over a rolling/non-fixed time window. The meaning was still discussed, and the error is penalized solely under sub-item 1b; this item must not stack a second penalty onto the same mistake.

Deduct the full 2 points only when the concept of "cumulative" is left entirely unexplained — i.e. the answer never says, correctly or incorrectly, what a cumulative KPISet is or represents (for example, it only names `self.cumulative` as a variable or discusses `_compact_times()` without ever indicating what the cumulative set is).
1b: Apply this sub-item to the answer's description of what a cumulative KPISet is. Deduct the full 3 points if that description contains any materially incorrect characterization — the two cases named in the rubric (saying cumulative KPISets involve or remove duplicates, or that they aggregate over a non-fixed time period) are illustrative examples, not an exhaustive list, so any factual error of any kind about what a cumulative KPISet is triggers the deduction. In particular, treat statements that the cumulative KPISet aggregates data over the whole test run, from the start of the test to the present moment, or over a growing/expanding window as asserting aggregation over a non-fixed time period, and deduct on that basis. Do not deduct only when the answer's characterization of cumulative KPISets is accurate throughout.
2a:
**Sub-item 2a (1 point): "_compact_times() performs memory optimization by combining elements."**

Award the point if the answer anywhere conveys *either* prong of the idea — that `_compact_times()` is a memory/size-reduction optimization, *or* that it combines/merges elements so the stored data structure shrinks. Both prongs together are not required; either one on its own is enough. It also does not matter how prominently or confidently the idea is stated: a hedged or incidental mention counts just as much as a flat assertion of the function's purpose. Phrasing such as "this presumably merges points to limit memory," or the point surfacing only as an aside inside a discussion of the per-KPISet overhead or of the cumulative merge, is sufficient for no_deduct.

Deduct the point only when neither prong appears: the answer ignores `_compact_times()` altogether, or describes it in some unrelated way. In particular, deduct when the answer attributes the call *solely* to making the statistics come out right — framing compaction as a prerequisite for "accurate" or "proper" averages, percentiles and standard deviation, or for "data integrity" — with no notion anywhere that it shrinks or merges the stored data.
2b: Apply this sub-item as a check on whether the answer mischaracterizes what `_compact_times()` actually does. Deduct the 2 points if the answer gives an incorrect account of its behavior — for example, describing it as removing or merging duplicates — and, in particular, deduct whenever the answer ties `_compact_times()` to statistical processing in any way at all, not merely when it claims the compaction is required or necessary for correct statistics. That means a deduction applies if the answer says the method prepares, normalizes, bins or rounds the data for percentile or aggregate computation, or says that percentiles or other aggregates are computed over the compacted data, or otherwise assigns it a role in the statistical pipeline, however hedged or incidental that framing is. Do not deduct only when the answer frames `_compact_times()` purely as a memory- or size-bounding operation — a space optimization that keeps the number of stored elements under a cap by combining them — with no statistical-processing role attributed to it. Note also that saying `_compact_times()` only has an effect on datasets with more elements than the maximum is correct and is not grounds for deduction here.
2c:
**2c — Overhead of calling `_compact_times()` on every KPISet (1 point)**

Award no deduction only if the answer explicitly identifies an actual cost or trade-off incurred by running `_compact_times()` repeatedly — for example CPU time, extra processing work, slowdown, a performance penalty, or wasted/redundant work on every merge. The cost must be named as a cost; it is not enough for the answer to observe that `_compact_times()` is invoked on or for every KPISet, or that it runs during each merge, if no cost of that repetition is identified. Likewise, an answer that raises the question only to dismiss it — arguing the overhead is negligible, or that the call is a cheap no-op for small datasets (e.g., when the number of elements is below the maximum) — has not established that calling `_compact_times()` on every KPISet imposes an overhead, and still receives the deduction. Deduct the 1 point in all such cases: silence about the repeated calls, bare mention of the repeated calls without any cost, or a claim that the repeated calls cost essentially nothing.
